abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly stand in for human participants, yet a plausible response is not evidence of a human decision process. The gap matters most when agents interact, where locally reasonable choices compound through delays and feedback into collective outcomes. Behavioral models fit decision rules to human data; we ask whether their qualitative content alone can drive LLM agents, an approach we call cognitive grounding. Here we show, across 231 sessions of the Beer Distribution Game, a supply-chain experiment in which players' orders amplify demand swings, that grounding moves seven LLMs toward human-calibrated behavior. Ungrounded agents reproduce the game's instability but miss its magnitude, timing and propagation; grounding improves trajectory fit for every model and generally shifts inferred decision parameters toward the human-calibrated reference, although unevenly across roles and models. The effect holds against independent empirical data and under alternative prompting and memory designs. Cognitively grounded LLMs are therefore candidate behavioral surrogates, contingent on task-specific validation.
